summaries.example: Imagine a group of students using the same kind of map to find places in a park. They keep finding paths the map does not explain. Someone makes a new map that changes what counts as a path and helps the group explore differently. Scientists can face a similar change, although real scientific changes are much more complicated.
summaries.summary: A scientific revolution is a major transformation in science. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry explains that people do not agree on exactly what this means or which episodes deserve the name. Thomas Kuhn gave the most discussed account. In his early picture, scientists usually do “normal science,” solving puzzles within a shared paradigm. Difficult problems called anomalies can build up. If confidence falls and a promising alternative appears, the field may undergo a paradigm change. The new approach can change important concepts, methods, goals, and even how scientists see the subject. Kuhn called some old and new approaches “incommensurable,” meaning they cannot be compared in every simple, shared way. Other thinkers emphasize gradual development, new instruments, better practices, or the way several specialties grow apart or combine. So scientific change can be both inventive and connected to tradition. The entry asks whether revolutions are necessary for progress, whether science moves toward truth, and whether all revolutions have one pattern.
key_ideas: Scientists disagree about which changes should count as true revolutions.
A revolution may change ideas, methods, tools, goals, or the way a scientific community works.
Thomas Kuhn described a pattern involving normal science, problems, crisis, and a possible new way of working.
Some historians see more continuity: new science often grows from older work instead of suddenly replacing it.
A change may look quick from far away but take many years when examined closely.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand that science is not just a list of facts. It is also a human activity in which people choose problems, use tools, share standards, and sometimes reorganize their work. Learning about revolutions can make us more careful when someone says that a new discovery changes everything. It also shows why history and philosophy can help explain how scientific knowledge develops.

important_terms.definition: A big change in how scientists understand a subject, investigate it, or organize their work.
A shared set of examples, ideas, and ways of working that guides scientists in a field.
A result that does not fit well with the accepted ideas or methods.
The study of how knowledge and scientific ideas change over time.

questions_to_think_about: Can a big improvement count as a revolution if it does not replace an old idea?
Why might scientists keep using an old way of thinking even when it has problems?
Does a new scientific idea always make science progress?
How could new tools change science without changing its main theory?

summaries.example: The transition from classical mechanics to relativity is often treated as revolutionary, but it illustrates why the label is debated. The new theory changed concepts such as mass and altered the framework used to describe physical phenomena. Yet it also addressed many related problems and preserved important connections with earlier mechanics. One interpretation therefore emphasizes conceptual discontinuity; another emphasizes continuity through shared problems, limiting cases, or inherited practices.
summaries.summary: The philosophical problem of scientific revolutions concerns the character, causes, and significance of large-scale scientific change. The entry notes broad agreement that science has experienced transformative developments, alongside disagreement about whether any are revolutions in a strictly Kuhnian sense. In Kuhn’s early model, mature research is organized by a paradigm: shared exemplary problems, concepts, standards, and practices. Normal science develops this framework but also uncovers anomalies. When persistent anomalies weaken confidence and an alternative attracts a substantial part of the community, a revolution or paradigm change may occur. Such a change is not simply the accumulation of observations. It can reorganize the field’s ontology, vocabulary, goals, methods, and social structure. Kuhn’s claim that rival paradigms may be incommensurable raised questions about whether theory choice is fully governed by common rules and whether scientific progress is cumulative or directed toward truth. Later Kuhn softened the picture, describing revolutions more as the formation of new specialties, comparable to biological speciation. Other approaches reject or limit Kuhn’s model. Continuity theorists emphasize inherited problems and practices; practice-centered accounts stress instruments and skills; broader historical accounts examine deep cultural frameworks. The central lesson is that “revolution” is a contested explanatory concept, not a label whose meaning can be assumed.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes the fact of transformative scientific development from the stronger claim that such development is revolutionary in Kuhn’s strict sense.
Kuhn’s early model presents normal science, persistent anomalies, crisis, and paradigm change as a recurring pattern in mature sciences.
A Kuhnian revolution can reorganize concepts, meanings, methods, values, research problems, practices, and scientific communities, not merely add new facts.
Kuhn’s claims about incommensurability and noncumulative progress created disputes about rationality, objectivity, realism, and relativism.
Alternative accounts stress continuity, changes in instruments and practices, nonlinear effects, or the splitting and recombination of specialties.
Kuhn’s later work treated revolutions more like scientific speciation: fields divide into specialties whose communication may become locally limited.
summaries.why_it_matters: How we describe scientific change affects how we understand evidence, progress, objectivity, and the relationship between history and philosophy of science. The topic also challenges a simple picture in which a timeless scientific method steadily adds facts. Studying competing accounts encourages careful distinctions: conceptual change may differ from practical change; rapid change may still have a long history; and a successful successor may both disrupt and depend on earlier work.

important_terms.definition: A profound transformation in scientific concepts, practices, standards, communities, or institutions; its exact criteria are disputed.
In Kuhn’s early account, a framework of exemplary problem-solutions and practices that organizes normal research.
A persistent result or problem that resists solution within an accepted scientific framework.
A relation in which rival frameworks lack a fully shared measure because meanings, standards, or classifications differ.
Research carried out within an accepted framework, usually by solving specialized puzzles rather than questioning the framework itself.
The view that major scientific change develops through links to earlier work rather than a sharp break.

questions_to_think_about: Should a revolution require a crisis in the earlier framework, or can improved instruments and practices be enough?
If a successor framework retains some successful results of its predecessor, is the change still noncumulative?
Does local incommensurability among specialties threaten the objectivity of science, or can it support more specialized progress?
Are revolutions causes of scientific progress, retrospective labels, or both?
How does the time scale chosen by a historian affect whether a development looks revolutionary or evolutionary?

summaries.example: Suppose a school’s robotics club uses one design plan. Most meetings involve solving small problems within that plan. Over time, the robots keep failing in ways the plan cannot explain. A new design system changes the parts, the testing rules, and what counts as a good solution. Some students may see it as a complete break; others may point out that the new system still uses older parts and lessons. Scientists can disagree in a similar way about whether a change is revolutionary.
summaries.summary: Scientific revolutions are large changes in science, but the entry shows that the idea is harder to define than it first appears. People generally agree that science has undergone important transformations. They disagree about whether these changes were sudden breaks, long developments, or different kinds of change that should not all receive the same label. Thomas Kuhn’s account is central. He describes mature science as organized around a paradigm, a shared framework that supplies examples, questions, methods, and standards. During normal science, researchers solve puzzles inside that framework. Their work can also reveal anomalies. If important anomalies persist, a crisis may develop. A competing framework may then attract enough scientists to produce a paradigm shift. The new framework can alter scientific language, goals, methods, standards, practices, and community organization. Kuhn’s idea of incommensurability suggests that old and new frameworks may not be judged by exactly the same standards, which led to debates about rationality and progress. Other historians and philosophers emphasize continuity: innovators often rely on earlier work, and some transformations involve tools, institutions, or improved techniques more than a new worldview. Kuhn later compared revolutions to the splitting of biological species into separate specialties. Thus, scientific change may involve both rupture and inheritance, and no single pattern is accepted for every case.
key_ideas: The phrase “scientific revolution” can describe changes in theories, methods, instruments, institutions, or scientific communities.
Kuhn’s influential account says that normal science may produce anomalies, leading to crisis and sometimes a paradigm shift.
A paradigm shift can change what questions matter, what methods are trusted, and what scientists think the world contains.
Critics argue that many important changes are gradual, depend on earlier traditions, or improve practice without overturning basic concepts.
Kuhn’s later view placed more emphasis on fields dividing into specialties, rather than one giant framework always being replaced by another.
The entry treats scientific progress as an open philosophical question, not as something with one universally accepted explanation.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate matters because it changes how we picture science. If science always grows by adding facts to one stable method, revolutions are difficult to explain. If every new framework makes older knowledge irrelevant, scientific progress and rational comparison become difficult to explain. Studying the debate gives us a more careful view: scientific communities can preserve traditions, discover unexpected problems, develop new tools, and reorganize their concepts in several different ways.

important_terms.definition: A major transformation in scientific understanding or practice; philosophers disagree about how large or sudden it must be.
A shared framework of examples, concepts, questions, and methods that guides a scientific community.
A puzzling observation or problem that does not fit the accepted framework.
A period when serious problems make researchers question the accepted framework and consider alternatives.
A deep mismatch between frameworks that makes their concepts, standards, or classifications difficult to compare directly.
The ordinary work of solving specialized problems within an accepted paradigm.

questions_to_think_about: Is a change revolutionary because it happens quickly, because it is deep, or because it affects a whole community?
Why might a scientific community protect an established paradigm?
Can a new theory be both different from and connected to an older theory?
Would a new instrument count as revolutionary if scientists use it to solve old problems more accurately?
Why might historians disagree about whether one large “Scientific Revolution” really occurred?
